title: Legal(tech) Briefs: Zach Posner ft. Mitch Zuklie (Chair, Orrick)
author: Mitch Zuklie · Zach Posner

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Repeatable services: Organisational redesign changes legal delivery
st.an: Zuklie shifts the emphasis from organisational redesign around repeatable AI-delivered services to an incumbent firm’s incremental adoption path: widespread assistance, bottom-up experimentation, proprietary data and responsiveness to sophisticated buyers. He explicitly says Orrick has not yet reached transformation, augmentation or automation, while leaving those later stages open.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: Zuklie accepts the work-redesign logic and materially extends it with law-firm operating-model examples: sophisticated in-house buyers drive disaggregation and continual service improvement, while digitisation removes administrative tasks and shifts associates toward greater substantive experience. His claims support task reallocation and organisational redesign, though they do not address AI’s jagged capabilities or verification requirements directly.

st.t: Delivery economics: AI pressures pricing and apprenticeship
st.an: Zuklie supports the cluster’s buyer-driven delivery proposition: sophisticated in-house legal, procurement and legal-operations functions increasingly press firms to improve efficiency, disaggregate work and deliver greater value. His prediction that proprietary datasets will become a competitive asset also aligns with the cluster’s emphasis on institutional data and incumbent advantages, though he does not address pricing, verification or apprenticeship directly.

st.t: In-house adoption: Stronger buyers may insource selectively
st.an: Zuklie supports the cluster’s stronger-buyer thesis: larger in-house teams, legal operations and procurement functions are driving value, scrutinising efficiency and disaggregating work, which pressures providers to improve. However, he does not specifically establish AI-driven insourcing, substitution for outside counsel or reduced external spending.

st.t: Service model: AI challenges production more than lawyers
st.an: Zuklie supports the cluster’s view that legal-service competition is being reshaped by technology, proprietary data and increasingly sophisticated buyers. He specifically reinforces the buyer-side reallocation point: stronger in-house, procurement and legal-operations functions pursue efficiency, diversify providers and disaggregate work, requiring law firms to improve delivery continuously. He does not directly address bounded automation, hybrid pricing or autonomous legal delivery.

kp.k: Technology strategy must address clients and firm operations
kp.d: Zuklie argues that technology adoption is accelerating, but law-firm leaders still face the same two strategic questions as in 1996: how technology changes clients' needs and therefore practice and recruitment priorities, and how it changes the firm's talent management and service delivery.
qs: the acceleration and the adoption things happen much more quickly than they did in the 1990s
the first is how does this technology affect our clients and therefore how do we have to focus our practice and the talent we're adding
how does it affect the way that we run our firm

kp.k: Generative AI arrives amid regulatory uncertainty and harsher enforcement
kp.d: In contrast to his experience of Silicon Valley in 1996, Zuklie describes contemporary technological innovation as closely entangled with government. He believes regulators, particularly federal regulators, are not keeping pace with innovation, leaving clients seeking guidance amid greater uncertainty, harsher enforcement against big technology companies and public skepticism. This is his assessment of the environment surrounding generative AI, not a measured regulatory finding.
qs: I don't think federal and state uh Regulators particularly Federal Regulators are keeping Pace with uh the the The Innovation that's happening
there's more gray area at the same time the enforcement World particularly I think for big tech companies is more harsh
The View on Main Street about big Tech is more skeptical than it's been at any time in my career

kp.k: Client advisory work informs internal generative AI adoption
kp.d: Zuklie presents Orrick's financing, exits, litigation and responsible-policy work as a source of practical understanding that informs its own use of generative AI. He reports more than $22 billion in financings over the past couple of years and involvement in five of the largest exits in the context of discussing this technological wave; these are interview claims rather than independently substantiated results.
qs: we've I think we've done more than $22 billion dollar in financings in the past couple years
we've worked on some of the largest exits I think uh on five of the largest exits
it's given us a window to think how we use gen in our own business

kp.k: Firm datasets may become a competitive differentiator
kp.d: Zuklie argues that technology already matters alongside brand, clients and culture in competition, including recruitment. He predicts that firms will soon also compete on their datasets because these could influence service quality and quantitative rigor. He does not provide comparative performance evidence for that prediction.
qs: we're going to compete not only in the basis of Our Brands and our clients and our culture but also in part on our technology
part of what we'll be competing on as our data set because I think it will be relevant to how we provide services and the quality and the quantitative rigor

kp.k: Sophisticated buyers pressure firms to improve efficiency and value
kp.d: Zuklie identifies larger, more capable in-house legal functions, procurement professionals and legal operations teams as a major difference from earlier technology waves. He argues that these buyers actively seek efficiency, diversify firms and disaggregate work, requiring providers to improve delivery, value and internal technological decisions.
qs: clients have sophisticated in-house legal operations with procurement folks
they are driving value from the from the client side more than they ever used to
how can I uh diversify the firms we're working with how do I disaggregate the work that's getting done
all of that means we need to perpetually get better

kp.k: Global integration prioritizes expertise over office proximity
kp.d: Zuklie explains that Orrick's lack of a global headquarters is an organizational choice intended to support dispersed leadership and integrated matter staffing, rather than a claim that industry centers no longer matter. He favors maintaining relevant geographic presences while selecting the best expertise across offices. This describes the firm's existing structure, not an AI-induced restructuring.
qs: we're going to put the best people around the world on that matter
we like the idea of thinking of ourselves as an integrated firm
we start by thinking what's best for the client not who's the person that's you know two doors down the down the hall for me

kp.k: Daily AI use is substantial but still assistive
kp.d: At the interview date, Zuklie estimates that about 60% of Orrick lawyers and about half its staff use its homegrown tool daily. Lawyer uses include proofreading, basic research, drafting and checklists; business-development uses include gathering data and drafting emails. He explicitly characterizes this as assistance, not yet augmentation, automation or firm transformation.
qs: literally 60% of our of our lawyers are using it on a daily basis
I think about half our staff uh ballpark
from basic proof reading to you know basic research to Drafting and coming up with checklists
I don't think we're yet augmenting or automating our work
it's assisting us it is not it is not any way transforming us yet

kp.k: Bottom-up experimentation guides training and product development
kp.d: Zuklie describes prompt sharing, observation of use and peer feedback as mechanisms for improving adoption and determining functionality, monthly updates and training. He reports positive informal feedback about efficiency and quality, especially from those responsible for drafting and research, but supplies no quantified productivity or quality evaluation. More extensive RFP support and data use remain aspirations.
qs: sharing prompts
observing how the team is using the tools and encouraging folks to share feedback with one another
what new functionality we want to add what we should be doing in monthly drops
it's helping us uh be more efficient and improves quality
it is for the most part A Bottoms Up not top down exercise

kp.k: Historical automation offers an optimistic training analogy
kp.d: Zuklie contrasts his early-career document copying, packaging, courier dispatch and manual closing checks with electronic delivery and signatures. He estimates that today's average associate probably handles 50% more deals per year than he did, allowing more substantive repetitions and stronger pattern recognition. This is a personal historical comparison supporting his optimism about AI, not a measured AI productivity effect.
qs: I spent three nights a week from six o'clock to 10 o'clock
that whole process which was a lot of hours a lot of painful hours you know um has disappeared
the average associate today because they're not dealing with all all of that uh grunt work probably is doing 50% more deals per year than I did
more chops and at bats at substantive work

kp.k: Talent changes depend on progress beyond assistance
kp.d: Zuklie says it is too early to know how fundamentally AI will alter the talent model because outcomes depend on the movement from assistance to augmentation and automation. His optimistic forecast is that change over the next couple of years could resemble the scale of improvement over his preceding 30 years: greater efficiency, faster experience accumulation, more data for judgment and increased importance of interpersonal skills. He hopes senior lawyers will have more time for mentoring and coaching, while explicitly acknowledging uncertainty.
qs: it's too early to know how fundamentally it changes the talent model
it's probably on the same scale over the next couple years of what I saw over the 30 years from when I started to now
it probably makes interpersonal skills more important
Associates are going to have the opportunity to gain experience and Reps much more quickly
I hope that that means that that frees people up to spend more time mentoring and coaching at the more senior levels as well

kp.k: The 2030 commission connects foresight to near-term changes
kp.d: Zuklie describes a commission of roughly 18 members, mostly junior partners with a few senior partners providing historical context. Its remit is to define the desired firm in 2030 and identify changes to begin in 2025 across talent, training, structure, technology, client service and the firm's model. Keeping its membership stable through the next five years is an intention; the interview does not report completed recommendations or outcomes.
qs: the 2030 commission was set up to uh identify roughly 18
it's mostly Junior Partners we have a couple senior Partners on there
what changes do we need to start implementing an Orc in 2025 in order to become the firm that they want to practice at in 2030
we're trying to keep the composition of this of this commission the same this year and through the next five years
what skills should we be hiring for what training should we do that's different

kp.k: Adaptability and interpersonal skills matter beyond technical specialization
kp.d: Asked about skills for younger generations, Zuklie cautions that increasing technological innovation does not necessarily make recruiting primarily for technological talent the right strategy. He favors broad thinking, adaptability, historical perspective and interpersonal capabilities. His accompanying career advice emphasizes brief weekly self-reflection and quarterly review to identify meaningful work, learn from mistakes and pursue better-fitting assignments.
qs: people who are technologically talented uh because there's going to be more technological innovation is not necessarily the right way to go
finding people who are able to think and deal with change
people with lots of inter you know interpersonal skills
three minutes a week with some you know quarterly self-reflection is a really helpful way to think about how to position yourself no matter what job you're in

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Mitch Zuklie describes current generative AI use at Orrick as useful assistance, not transformation, and predicts stronger effects on competition, service delivery and lawyer development as capabilities advance.
pts.d: Zuklie reports daily use of Orrick's homegrown tool by approximately 60% of lawyers and about half of staff. Uses include proofreading, basic research, drafting, checklists, business-development data gathering and draft emails. He says users report greater efficiency and improved quality, with somewhat more time for creative and thoughtful input rather than routine work. Adoption is primarily bottom-up, particularly among people responsible for drafting and research. He explicitly distinguishes this present 'assist' stage from future augmentation and automation, and hopes for more substantial support for requests for proposals and data-informed responses. He predicts that firms will compete partly on their datasets, alongside technology, because data will influence service quality and quantitative rigor. He expects AI-enabled efficiency to let associates accumulate substantive experience more quickly, give lawyers more data for judgment calls and increase the importance of interpersonal skills. More senior time for mentoring and coaching is a hope, not a reported outcome. In the broader context surrounding generative AI, he argues that regulatory uncertainty and harsher enforcement create client demand for guidance, while sophisticated in-house legal and procurement teams pressure firms to improve efficiency and value. His hiring view favors adaptability, broad thinking and interpersonal abilities rather than assuming technological specialization alone is the right response.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence offered consists of Zuklie's internal adoption estimates, qualitative user feedback, client-work experience and analogies with earlier technological changes; future effects are his expectations.
pts.d: The approximate adoption figures are speaker-reported, without a stated measurement method or observation period. Efficiency and quality claims rest on informal feedback and observation rather than quantified output, time-saving or quality measures. Zuklie says the firm learns from usage and shared prompts to guide functionality and training. He grounds his understanding of generative AI partly in advising clients: he cites more than $22 billion in financings over the preceding couple of years, major exits including Casetext's sale to Thomson Reuters, litigation and responsible-policy work. These are credentials and experience claims, not tests of AI's productivity effects. For lawyer development, he compares his early career's physical document handling with electronic delivery and signatures today. He estimates that contemporary associates do about 50% more deals annually than he did, using this historical technology analogy to anticipate faster experience accumulation with AI; the estimate is not presented as a measured generative AI outcome. No formal benchmark or controlled study is cited. Dataset-based competition, future augmentation and automation, and mentoring benefits are predictions or hopes.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Zuklie places current use in the early assistance stage, forecasts potentially substantial change over the next couple of years, and describes planning from 2025 toward 2030 without treating that horizon as a guaranteed automation deadline.
pts.d: At the time of the interview, Zuklie says AI is saving time but is not yet life-changing or transformational for Orrick. Augmentation and automation are stages he expects to follow, without assigning them firm dates. He tentatively predicts that the scale of change over the next couple of years could resemble the change he experienced over the previous 30 years. He expressly says it is too early to know the fundamental effect on the talent model: it depends on how far work moves along the assistance–augmentation–automation spectrum. Workflow design is an important condition for clients and teams to realize benefits. Dataset-based competition is expected 'soon' in an imprecisely transcribed phrase. Orrick's 2030 commission is a planning mechanism: a mainly junior-partner group is considering the desired future firm and changes to begin implementing in 2025, with intended continuity of membership over five years. Its remit includes talent, training, structure, technology and client service; it is not evidence that any particular future staffing model has already been selected.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The claims chiefly concern Orrick and comparable corporate law firms, their lawyers and staff, and sophisticated corporate clients rather than consumer legal services.
pts.d: Lawyers doing substantial drafting and research are identified as leading current adoption. Associates are expected to gain more substantive repetitions and develop judgment faster as routine work diminishes. Senior lawyers may have more capacity for mentoring, although Zuklie does not report that this has happened. Staff and business-development professionals obtain help with data collection and communications. Firm leaders face decisions about technology, proprietary datasets, training, recruitment and workflow design to maintain competitive service quality and value. Corporate clients are both recipients of potentially better legal services and buyers applying pressure through increasingly sophisticated in-house counsel, legal operations and procurement. Companies navigating data-driven innovation, particularly big technology companies, also need regulatory guidance in an uncertain enforcement environment; this is presented as the context into which generative AI arrives, not solely an effect caused by AI. Prospective recruits may benefit from adaptability and interpersonal skills. Zuklie does not predict specific headcount reductions, changes in associate-to-partner ratios, or access-to-justice outcomes.
